subject: ethereum
question: Who proposed Ethereum, and when was the original whitepaper written?
options: Vitalik Buterin, then 19 years old, conceived the idea in late 2013 and published the whitepaper in 2014, before the network's 2015 launch
A large bank invented Ethereum in the 1990s
Satoshi Nakamoto created both Bitcoin and Ethereum together
Ethereum has no known founder or origin
explanation: Vitalik Buterin conceived Ethereum's core idea in late 2013 and published the whitepaper in 2014. Ethereum had eight co-founders total, including Gavin Wood (who wrote the technical 'Yellow Paper' and created the Solidity language).

subject: ethereum
question: When did the Ethereum network officially launch (the 'Frontier' release)?
options: January 3, 2009
September 15, 2022
October 31, 2008
explanation: Ethereum's mainnet went live on July 30, 2015, under the codename 'Frontier' — roughly a year and a half after the whitepaper was published and after a 2014 public crowdsale that raised funding in Bitcoin.

subject: ethereum
question: How did Ethereum's original vision differ from Bitcoin's, as described in Ethereum's own whitepaper?
options: Ethereum aimed to be a general-purpose, programmable 'world computer' supporting a wide range of applications, not just peer-to-peer currency transactions
Ethereum's whitepaper described an identical goal to Bitcoin's whitepaper with no distinction
Ethereum was designed exclusively as a faster version of email
Ethereum's original goal was to replace all internet browsers
explanation: While Bitcoin was purpose-built for peer-to-peer electronic cash, Ethereum's whitepaper proposed a programmable blockchain capable of running arbitrary code (smart contracts), enabling a much broader range of applications beyond simple payments.

subject: ethereum
question: How do smart contracts on Ethereum specifically work, building on the general concept from the Blockchain subject?
options: Developers write smart contract code (commonly in Solidity) that gets deployed to and executed by the Ethereum network itself, with the results recorded on-chain
Ethereum smart contracts are only theoretical and have never actually been deployed on the network
Smart contracts on Ethereum require a lawyer to manually approve every execution
Ethereum doesn't support smart contracts; that's a feature exclusive to other networks
explanation: Ethereum was the first major blockchain to make smart contracts broadly practical and widely used — Solidity is the most common programming language for writing them, and deployed contracts run automatically according to their code.

subject: ethereum
question: What is the EVM (Ethereum Virtual Machine)?
options: The runtime environment that executes smart contract code consistently across every node on the Ethereum network
A physical computer manufactured by the Ethereum Foundation
A cryptocurrency exchange platform
A term with no real technical function
explanation: The EVM ensures that smart contract code executes identically and deterministically on every participating node, which is essential for the network to reach consensus on the results of contract execution.

subject: ethereum
question: What is Solidity?
options: The most widely used programming language for writing Ethereum smart contracts, created by Gavin Wood
The name of Ethereum's native cryptocurrency
A hardware wallet brand
A consensus mechanism used by Ethereum
explanation: Solidity is a purpose-built language designed for writing smart contracts that run on the EVM — since its creation, it has become the dominant language in Ethereum smart contract development.

subject: ethereum
question: What is 'ETH' (Ether)?
options: The native cryptocurrency of the Ethereum network, used to pay for transactions and computation (gas), among other uses
A stablecoin pegged to the US dollar
The name of Ethereum's official corporate entity
A synonym for Bitcoin
explanation: ETH is Ethereum's native asset — beyond being a tradeable currency, it also serves the essential functional role of paying for computation and storage (gas fees) on the network.

subject: ethereum
question: How does the general 'gas fee' concept (introduced in the Blockchain subject) apply specifically to Ethereum?
options: Every operation performed by a smart contract or transaction on Ethereum consumes 'gas,' paid in ETH, with more complex operations costing more gas
Ethereum has no fee mechanism of any kind, unlike other blockchains
Gas fees on Ethereum are always a single, permanently fixed amount that never changes
Gas exclusively refers to fuel used to power Ethereum's physical mining hardware
explanation: Gas measures computational effort — simple transfers cost less gas than complex smart contract interactions — and gas prices fluctuate based on network demand, which is why fees can vary significantly over time.

subject: ethereum
question: How does Ethereum's account-based model for tracking balances differ from Bitcoin's UTXO model (covered in the Bitcoin subject)?
options: Ethereum tracks a simple running balance per account, similar to a bank account; Bitcoin tracks discrete unspent transaction outputs that get consumed and recombined
Ethereum and Bitcoin use the exact same balance-tracking model with no differences
Ethereum has no way of tracking balances at all
Bitcoin uses an account model, while Ethereum uses the UTXO model
explanation: This is a genuine architectural difference between the two networks — Ethereum's account model is generally considered more intuitive for supporting complex smart contract state, while Bitcoin's UTXO model has different tradeoffs suited to its simpler transaction-focused design.

subject: ethereum
question: What is the ERC-20 token standard?
options: A widely-adopted technical standard defining a common set of rules for creating fungible tokens on Ethereum, allowing them to work consistently across wallets and applications
A physical Ethereum-branded credit card
A law requiring all Ethereum users to register with the government
A standard that applies exclusively to Bitcoin, not Ethereum
explanation: ERC-20 defines a common interface (like functions for checking balances and transferring tokens) that token creators follow, which is a major reason why so many different tokens can be supported consistently across the same wallets and exchanges.

subject: ethereum
question: How does the ERC-721 token standard differ from ERC-20?
options: ERC-721 defines 'non-fungible' tokens, where each token is unique and not interchangeable — unlike ERC-20's fungible, identical/interchangeable tokens
ERC-721 and ERC-20 are exactly the same standard with two different names
ERC-721 tokens cannot be transferred once created
ERC-721 only applies to physical, not digital, assets
explanation: Fungible tokens (ERC-20) are interchangeable, like currency units. Non-fungible tokens (ERC-721) each have unique properties or identity, commonly used to represent distinct digital items or collectibles.

subject: ethereum
question: On what date did Ethereum's 'Merge' — its transition from Proof of Work to Proof of Stake — occur?
options: September 15, 2022
August 2021
January 10, 2024
explanation: The Merge, completed on September 15, 2022, combined Ethereum's original execution layer with the Proof-of-Stake Beacon Chain (which had been running in parallel since December 2020), permanently ending Proof-of-Work mining on Ethereum.

subject: ethereum
question: What was one major measurable impact of Ethereum's Merge?
options: It reduced Ethereum's energy consumption by approximately 99.95%, since Proof of Stake doesn't require competitive computational mining
It increased Ethereum's energy consumption by 99.95%
It had no measurable effect on energy consumption whatsoever
It permanently doubled the maximum supply of ETH
explanation: This dramatic energy reduction, confirmed by the Ethereum Foundation itself, is one of the most cited outcomes of the Merge — Proof of Stake replaces competitive computational mining with a system based on staked capital.

subject: ethereum
question: Since the Merge, how does Ethereum select who validates transactions and proposes new blocks?
options: Through Proof of Stake — participants ('validators') who have staked ETH as collateral are selected to propose and validate blocks, replacing the previous mining-based process
Through the exact same Proof of Work mining process Ethereum has always used
Through a single central company that manually approves every block
Through a fixed, unchanging list of validators set at Ethereum's launch in 2015
explanation: Validators lock up ETH as stake and are chosen (with an element of randomness weighted by stake) to propose and attest to blocks — as documented on ethereum.org, validators replaced miners entirely after the Merge.

subject: ethereum
question: As of the current Ethereum protocol design, what is the minimum amount of ETH required to run an independent validator?
options: 32 ETH
1 ETH
0.01 ETH
explanation: Running a solo validator requires staking 32 ETH. Note this is a protocol parameter that could theoretically change through future upgrades, and various staking pool services also let people participate with smaller amounts by pooling funds together.

subject: ethereum
question: What change did EIP-1559 (part of the August 2021 London upgrade) introduce to Ethereum's fee structure?
options: It introduced a base fee that is algorithmically adjusted based on network demand and then burned (permanently removed from circulation), alongside an optional tip paid to validators
It eliminated all transaction fees on Ethereum entirely
It doubled every transaction fee permanently with no adjustment mechanism
It has no relationship to how Ethereum's fees work
explanation: EIP-1559 replaced Ethereum's previous first-price auction fee model with a more predictable base-fee-plus-tip system, where the base fee portion is burned rather than paid to validators — this burning mechanism can make ETH's net issuance lower, or even negative, during periods of high network usage.

subject: ethereum
question: Unlike Bitcoin's fixed 21 million cap (covered in the Bitcoin subject), does Ethereum have a hard maximum supply limit?
options: No — Ethereum does not have a fixed maximum supply cap built into its protocol the way Bitcoin does, though EIP-1559's fee-burning mechanism can offset new issuance, sometimes resulting in periods of net-negative supply growth
Yes, Ethereum has an identical 21 million coin hard cap, just like Bitcoin
Ethereum's supply is permanently frozen and has never changed since 2015
Ethereum's supply cap is exactly double Bitcoin's at 42 million
explanation: This is an important, sometimes-misunderstood distinction — Ethereum's monetary policy differs fundamentally from Bitcoin's fixed-cap design. Note that Ethereum's exact issuance mechanics have been adjusted through protocol upgrades over time and could continue to evolve through future governance.

subject: ethereum
question: What was 'The DAO,' and what significant event happened to it in 2016?
options: The DAO was an early, prominent decentralized investment fund built on Ethereum smart contracts; it suffered a major hack in 2016 that led to a highly contentious hard fork, splitting the network into Ethereum and Ethereum Classic
The DAO was a physical Ethereum office building that was robbed in 2016
The DAO was Ethereum's original name before being renamed in 2016
Nothing significant happened to The DAO; this is not a real historical event
explanation: The DAO hack exploited a vulnerability in its smart contract code, and the community's decision to hard-fork Ethereum to effectively reverse the theft was deeply controversial — the portion of the community that rejected this intervention continued the original chain as Ethereum Classic.

subject: ethereum
question: What does 'DAO' (Decentralized Autonomous Organization) mean as a general concept enabled by platforms like Ethereum?
options: An organization whose rules and fund management are largely encoded in smart contracts and governed by member voting, rather than by traditional centralized management
A government regulatory agency overseeing cryptocurrency
A synonym for any company that happens to accept cryptocurrency payments
A term with no real connection to smart contracts or blockchain technology
explanation: DAOs use smart contracts to encode organizational rules (like voting and treasury management), aiming for more transparent, member-driven governance than traditional organizational structures — the concept was popularized significantly by (though predates the failure of) The DAO example above.

subject: ethereum
question: What is an EIP (Ethereum Improvement Proposal)?
options: A formal document proposing new features, standards, or process changes for Ethereum, discussed openly by the community before potential implementation
A type of Ethereum wallet application
A mandatory registration required to use Ethereum
A term unrelated to how Ethereum's protocol evolves
explanation: EIPs are Ethereum's equivalent of Bitcoin's BIPs — a structured, public process for proposing and discussing protocol changes. EIP-1559 (covered above) is a well-known example of an EIP that was ultimately implemented.

subject: ethereum
question: What is the general role of the Ethereum Foundation?
options: A nonprofit organization that supports Ethereum's research, development, and ecosystem growth — though it doesn't unilaterally control the decentralized network itself
A for-profit company that owns exclusive rights to the Ethereum blockchain
A government agency responsible for regulating Ethereum globally
The sole entity capable of approving every Ethereum transaction
explanation: The Ethereum Foundation supports the ecosystem's development, but Ethereum's actual governance and operation is decentralized — no single entity, including the Foundation, unilaterally controls the network or forces changes onto it.

subject: ethereum
question: What is a 'dApp' (decentralized application)?
options: An application whose backend logic runs on a blockchain (often via smart contracts) rather than on servers controlled by a single central company
Any mobile app that can be downloaded from an app store
An application that has no connection to blockchain technology whatsoever
A synonym for a traditional, centrally-hosted website
explanation: dApps typically combine a conventional user interface with backend logic executed via smart contracts on a blockchain like Ethereum, reducing (though not always eliminating) reliance on a centralized company controlling the core logic.

subject: ethereum
question: In May 2024, what significant regulatory development occurred for Ethereum in the United States?
options: The SEC approved spot Ethereum ETF applications, following its earlier approval of spot Bitcoin ETFs in January 2024
The SEC banned all Ethereum-related financial products outright
Ethereum was declared illegal to own in the United States
This event did not actually happen
explanation: Following the January 2024 spot Bitcoin ETF approvals, the SEC issued approval for spot Ethereum ETF applications in May 2024, extending regulated, exchange-traded exposure to a second major cryptocurrency.

subject: ethereum
question: Why can Ethereum gas fees vary significantly at different times?
options: Fees respond to network demand — when many people want their transactions processed simultaneously, competition for limited block space drives fees higher, and they fall when demand is lower
Gas fees are set once at Ethereum's launch and have never changed since
Gas fees are entirely random with no relationship to network activity
Gas fees are fixed by a single government agency
explanation: This demand-driven fee volatility is a well-documented characteristic of Ethereum's base layer — it's a major motivation behind Layer 2 scaling solutions, which the Base subject explores in depth.

subject: ethereum
question: What's a fair, balanced way to compare Ethereum and Bitcoin's core design goals?
options: Bitcoin was designed primarily as peer-to-peer digital cash with a fixed monetary policy; Ethereum was designed as a broader programmable platform supporting smart contracts and diverse applications — different design goals rather than one being objectively 'better'
Ethereum and Bitcoin have always had identical goals and technical designs
Bitcoin is objectively useless compared to Ethereum in every possible way
Ethereum is objectively useless compared to Bitcoin in every possible way
explanation: Presenting this comparison evenhandedly matters — both networks have different founding goals and tradeoffs, and reasonable evaluations depend on what specific properties (security model, programmability, monetary policy) matter most for a given use case.

subject: ethereum
question: What was a key focus of Ethereum's Dencun upgrade (March 2024)?
options: Introducing 'blobs' — a new way to handle data availability — specifically aimed at reducing costs for Layer 2 networks built on top of Ethereum
Permanently reverting Ethereum back to Proof of Work mining
Eliminating gas fees on Ethereum entirely and permanently
Merging Ethereum with the Bitcoin network
explanation: Dencun's blob mechanism specifically targeted reducing data costs for Layer 2 rollups (like Base, covered in the next subject), reflecting Ethereum's ongoing strategy of scaling primarily through Layer 2 solutions rather than only base-layer changes.

subject: ethereum
question: Why has Ethereum's ecosystem increasingly relied on Layer 2 networks (a concept introduced generally in the Blockchain subject)?
options: To help address base-layer scalability and cost limitations, by processing many transactions off the main Ethereum chain while still relying on it for underlying security
Layer 2 networks have no actual relationship to Ethereum whatsoever
Layer 2 networks were created to replace Ethereum entirely and make it obsolete
Ethereum has never had any Layer 2 networks built on top of it
explanation: This sets up the next subject in the curriculum — Base is one prominent example of an Ethereum Layer 2 network, built specifically to address these scalability and cost considerations while inheriting Ethereum's underlying security.

subject: ethereum
question: How was Ethereum's initial development funded?
options: Through a 2014 public crowdsale (an early form of what's now often called an ICO), which raised funding paid in Bitcoin
Through a bank loan from a single traditional financial institution
Ethereum required no funding at all to develop
Through a government grant program
explanation: The 2014 crowdsale raised funding (commonly cited as around $18 million in Bitcoin) to support Ethereum's development ahead of its 2015 launch — an early and influential example of what later became widely known as an ICO (Initial Coin Offering).
